sections.skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Kai places a MARKET order to buy 10 shares. What does this mean?

choices.text: Buy only if the price falls to a set amount
Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
Buy at yesterday's closing price, guaranteed
Buy only after the market closes for the day

questions.correct_answer: Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
questions.intro: To buy an investment, you place an order with your broker. A market order asks to buy or sell right away at the best available price. It usually executes quickly, but the exact price is not guaranteed and can differ from the last price you saw, especially in fast markets.
questions.feedback: Market orders prioritize speed, not a guaranteed price.
questions.topic: Placing an order: market and limit orders
sources: SEC Investor.gov: A market order seeks immediate execution at the best available price, which is not guaranteed; a limit order sets a maximum purchase or minimum sale price and may not execute. questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Lia places a LIMIT order to buy at $50. The stock is trading at $52. What happens?

choices.text: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower
It buys immediately at $52
It buys at $52 and refunds $2
It buys at exactly $50 no matter what the market price is

questions.correct_answer: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower
questions.intro: A limit order sets the most you will pay (to buy) or the least you will accept (to sell). It executes only at the limit price or better, so it may not execute at all.
questions.feedback: A buy limit at $50 fills only at $50 or less.
questions.topic: Placing an order: market and limit orders

misconceptions.D: Thinks the limit forces a price

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stock shows: bid $49.95, ask $50.05. If Omar places a market order to BUY, about what price will he pay?
questions.intro: The bid is the highest price buyers are offering; the ask is the lowest price sellers will accept. Buyers usually pay the ask, and sellers receive the bid. The difference is the bid-ask spread.
questions.feedback: A market buy order typically fills near the ask, $50.05.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Using the bid of $49.95 and ask of $50.05, what is the bid-ask spread?
questions.intro: The bid-ask spread = ask − bid. Narrow spreads mean lower trading costs.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: In any market, who decides the price of a trade?

choices.text: A buyer and a seller who agree
Only the buyer, by bidding higher
The government
The bank

questions.correct_answer: A buyer and a seller who agree
questions.intro: A trade happens when a buyer and a seller agree on a price. Exchanges match buyers and sellers.
questions.feedback: Trades happen at prices both sides accept.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A seller asks $20 for a used game. A buyer offers $18. What must happen for a sale?

choices.text: The sale happens at $18 automatically
The sale happens at $20 automatically
One of them changes their price until they agree
The sale happens at $38, the two prices added together

questions.correct_answer: One of them changes their price until they agree
questions.intro: The asking price is what a seller wants; the offer (bid) is what a buyer will pay.
questions.feedback: No trade occurs until the bid and ask meet.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Ana owns a stock trading at $40. She places a SELL limit order at $45. When can it execute?

choices.text: Immediately at $40
Only if the price rises to $45 or higher
Only if the price falls to $45 or lower
At exactly $45, regardless of the market price

questions.correct_answer: Only if the price rises to $45 or higher
questions.intro: A sell limit order sets the minimum price you will accept. It executes only at that price or higher.
questions.feedback: A sell limit at $45 fills at $45 or more.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stop-loss (stop) order to sell at $35 becomes a market order when the price falls to $35. The price gaps down overnight to $30. What might happen?

choices.text: It sells at exactly $35, which is guaranteed by the order
It cancels itself automatically
It may sell near $30, below the $35 stop price
It buys more shares

questions.correct_answer: It may sell near $30, below the $35 stop price
questions.intro: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached, so the sale price can be worse than the stop price in a fast-moving market.
questions.feedback: Once triggered, it is a market order and fills at the next available price.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: An order marked "good 'til canceled" (GTC) means…

choices.text: it lasts only one minute
it is canceled at market open
it guarantees execution
it stays open until filled or canceled, up to the broker's time limit

questions.correct_answer: it stays open until filled or canceled, up to the broker's time limit
questions.intro: Orders can be day orders (expire at the end of the trading day) or good-'til-canceled (stay open longer, often up to a time limit set by the broker).
questions.feedback: GTC orders remain open until filled, canceled, or they expire under the broker's rules.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A long-term investor buys a widely traded index ETF with a narrow spread. Which order type is often reasonable?

choices.text: A limit order near the current ask, or a market order
A stop-loss order far below the price
A stop order far below the price
A sell limit order

questions.correct_answer: A limit order near the current ask, or a market order
questions.intro: For heavily traded funds with narrow spreads, market orders usually fill close to the quoted price, and a limit order at the ask adds price protection.
questions.feedback: Either works for liquid ETFs; a limit at the ask adds price protection.

questions.prompt: A thinly traded stock has a bid of $9.50 and an ask of $10.50. Kai buys 100 shares at the ask and immediately sells at the bid. How much does he lose?
questions.intro: A wide spread is a hidden trading cost: buying at the ask and selling at the bid loses the spread on each share.
